mechanical_counts.duplicate_or_near_duplicate_items: 6 topic clusters cover 37/44 items; 12 items are direct restatements of another item

worst_places.quote: Keys are not for styling, sorting, or persistence across renders—those are misconceptions.
worst_places.problem: react-quiz-17 declares state persistence a misconception and keys its option 4 wrong for saying it. But react-quiz-13's keyed-correct option is "...enabling correct state persistence across re-renders", react-quiz-27's is "...and preserving component state", react-quiz-47's is "...enabling proper state preservation across re-renders", and content/topics/react/en/05-fiber-and-reconciliation.md has a whole section titled "The key prop as an intentional reset mechanism". A reader who answers 13/27/47 correctly gets told in 17 that the same answer is a misconception. This is the single worst defect in the bank.
worst_places.before: Keys are not for styling, sorting, or persistence across renders—those are misconceptions.
worst_places.after: Keys are not for styling or sorting. They are also not a way to make state survive a page reload — that needs storage, not keys. What they do control is which existing component instance React reuses, and that is exactly what decides whether state stays with the right item.

worst_places.quote: Using array index as a key is always safe if the list is not filtered or reordered
worst_places.problem: react-quiz-47 keys this option WRONG. content/questions/react.json says the opposite in plain words: "for a genuinely static list that's harmless", and lists the exact preconditions (never reordered, filtered, or prepended; items have no local state). A reader who studied the question bank gets marked wrong for repeating it. The word «always» is the only thing arguably wrong here, and nothing in the explanation says so.
worst_places.before: Using array index as a key is always safe if the list is not filtered or reordered
worst_places.after: Using array index as a key is safe only if the list is never reordered, filtered or prepended AND its items hold no local state — three conditions people rarely check

worst_places.quote: Без стабильных ключей (таких как индексы массива) React может неправильно переиспользовать экземпляры компонентов, вызывая ошибки состояния и проблемы производительности.
worst_places.problem: The parenthesis attaches to «стабильных ключей», so the sentence literally reads "without stable keys, such as array indices" — i.e. it teaches that array indices ARE stable keys, the exact opposite of what react-quiz-2 and react-quiz-8 teach. The English original has the same ambiguity ("Without stable keys (like using array indices)"). A B1-B2 reader on a phone will take the sentence at face value.
worst_places.before: Без стабильных ключей (таких как индексы массива) React может неправильно переиспользовать экземпляры компонентов, вызывая ошибки состояния и проблемы производительности.
worst_places.after: Если ключи нестабильны — например, если вы взяли индекс массива — React может переиспользовать экземпляры компонентов не там, где нужно. Это даёт ошибки состояния и лишние рендеры.

worst_places.quote: Hooks must be called at the top level of a functional component on every render in the same order. Conditional calls (option 1), loops (option 3), and class methods (option 4) violate the Rules of Hooks. Only option 2 correctly shows useEffect being called consistently at the top level without conditional logic or loops.
worst_places.problem: react-quiz-18's whole explanation is written as a map from option numbers to verdicts. shuffleOptions in src/lib/quiz-utils.ts permutes options on the random-quiz route, so on that route every one of these four numbers points at the wrong option. Even on the per-topic route the numbering is 1-based while the UI shows no numbers, so the reader has to count. react-quiz-48 and -49 have the same problem.
worst_places.before: Conditional calls (option 1), loops (option 3), and class methods (option 4) violate the Rules of Hooks. Only option 2 correctly shows useEffect being called consistently at the top level without conditional logic or loops.
worst_places.after: Only one answer is correct: calling useEffect at the top level on every render. The other three each break a rule — a hook inside an if runs only sometimes, a hook inside a loop runs a different number of times per render, and a hook in a class method is not in a function component at all.

worst_places.quote: 'Effect ran' logged twice due to StrictMode, component renders with count=1
worst_places.problem: react-quiz-46 keys this option wrong, and react-quiz-32 keys the identical distractor «'mounted' twice due to strict mode» wrong. In React 18 development StrictMode this is exactly what happens — content/questions/react.json states it: "React 18 StrictMode mounts/unmounts/remounts each component once in dev". Neither item's stem or explanation says "in production" or "without StrictMode", so both items punish the reader for knowing the correct behaviour.
worst_places.before: The effect runs once after initial render because the dependency array is empty.
worst_places.after: In a production build the effect runs once after the first render, because the dependency array is empty. (In development with StrictMode React deliberately mounts, unmounts and remounts once, so you would see the log twice — this question asks about production.)

worst_places.quote: The effect runs synchronously on mount, so 'Fetching data' is logged first. The component renders with data=null, displaying 'Loading...'.
worst_places.problem: react-quiz-10. Two problems in two sentences. First, useEffect does not run synchronously on mount — it runs after the browser has painted; that is the whole point of useEffect vs useLayoutEffect. Second, the explanation's own narrative (render → 'Loading...' → then the fetch) matches distractor 2, which the item keys as wrong, while the keyed answer says 'Fetching data' comes first. The reader gets a factually wrong rule and a key that its own explanation undercuts.
worst_places.before: The effect runs synchronously on mount, so 'Fetching data' is logged first. The component renders with data=null, displaying 'Loading...'.
worst_places.after: React renders first: the component returns 'Loading...' because data is null. Only after that commit does the effect run, logging 'Fetching data'. The question asks about console output, so 'Fetching data' is the first line in the console.

worst_places.quote: Их основное преимущество — предотвращение ненужных пересчетов мемоизированных дочерних компонентов (обернутых в React.memo), которые зависят от этих props. Без стабильных ссылок, даже если логика не изменилась, дочерние компоненты будут пересчитываться на каждом рендере родителя.
worst_places.problem: react-quiz-4 ru. «Re-render» is translated twice as «пересчёт» (recalculation). Components are not recalculated, they are re-rendered, and the whole item is about the difference between recalculating a value and re-rendering a child — so the mistranslation destroys the one distinction the item teaches. The same file uses «перерендер» in react-quiz-12 and «повторный рендер» in react-quiz-49: three terms for one concept.
worst_places.before: Их основное преимущество — предотвращение ненужных пересчетов мемоизированных дочерних компонентов (обернутых в React.memo), которые зависят от этих props. Без стабильных ссылок, даже если логика не изменилась, дочерние компоненты будут пересчитываться на каждом рендере родителя.
worst_places.after: Их основное преимущество — не давать лишний раз перерендериваться дочерним компонентам, обёрнутым в React.memo и получающим эти props. Без стабильных ссылок такой компонент перерендерится на каждом рендере родителя, даже если логика не менялась.

worst_places.quote: Пропа key критична для согласованности—она помогает React сопоставить старые элементы с новыми при перерендерах.
worst_places.problem: react-quiz-27 ru. Three errors in nine words: «пропа» (the term is masculine, «проп»), «согласованности» = consistency, but the English is "reconciliation" = «согласование» — a different concept, and the reader has no way to recover the right one. Across the bank the same term appears as «Prop key» (quiz-2, -24, -37), «Пропс key» (quiz-17), «Пропа key» (quiz-27) and «prop key» — four spellings of one word.
worst_places.before: Пропа key критична для согласованности—она помогает React сопоставить старые элементы с новыми при перерендерах.
worst_places.after: Проп key нужен для согласования (reconciliation) — процесса, в котором React сопоставляет старые элементы с новыми при перерендере.

worst_places.quote: Управляемый компонент имеет его значение явно управляемое состоянием React. Обработчик onChange должен обновить состояние, и это значение состояния должно быть передано в props value.
worst_places.problem: react-quiz-34 ru. Word-for-word calque of "A controlled component has its value explicitly managed by React state": «имеет его значение» is not Russian, and two unagreed participles («явно управляемое») stack onto the subject. «передано в props value» should be «в проп value». The first sentence of the explanation is the highest-weight position in the rubric and it is the least readable sentence in the file.
worst_places.before: Управляемый компонент имеет его значение явно управляемое состоянием React. Обработчик onChange должен обновить состояние, и это значение состояния должно быть передано в props value.
worst_places.after: У управляемого компонента значением владеет состояние React. Обработчик onChange обновляет состояние, а это состояние передаётся обратно в проп value.

worst_places.quote: useMemo и useCallback предназначены для сохранения референциального равенства значений и функций между рендерами.
worst_places.problem: «Референциальное равенство» is a transliteration, not a Russian term, and it is never explained anywhere in the file — yet it is the load-bearing idea of eight items (4, 15, 20, 25, 35, 40, 45, 49). DOM has the same problem: it appears 12 times across 6 items and is never expanded. Every item is read standalone in a quiz, so "it is explained in the article" does not help.
worst_places.before: useMemo и useCallback предназначены для сохранения референциального равенства значений и функций между рендерами.
worst_places.after: useMemo и useCallback нужны, чтобы между рендерами возвращалась та же самая ссылка на значение или функцию, а не новая копия (это и называют referential equality — равенство по ссылке).

patterns: Answer-shape bias makes the whole bank guessable without reading the question. correctIndex is 0 in 34/44 and 1 in 10/44 — never 2 or 3 — and the correct option is the longest one in 31/44. Because shuffleOptions is applied only on the random-quiz route, on the per-topic route the reader sees the correct answer first and longest, every single time. Two of the three tell-tales are in the data itself: the correct option is the only one that carries a second clause ("...enabling correct state persistence", "...while an uncontrolled component manages its own value via the DOM"), and the distractors are one-liners.

The bank is six restated questions, not 44. Ten items ask what the key prop is for (2, 8, 13, 17, 22, 24, 27, 33, 37, 47), eight ask useMemo vs useCallback (4, 15, 20, 25, 35, 40, 45, 49), ten log render/effect order (3, 7, 10, 12, 16, 26, 32, 38, 42, 46), five ask controlled vs uncontrolled (5, 14, 19, 34, 48), four ask the Rules of Hooks (1, 11, 41, 18) — 37 of 44 items. Inside those clusters items 1/11/41 are the same code with a renamed condition, 42/46 the same code with one extra console.log, and 12/16/26 the same counter. The restatements are also where the contradictions come from: with ten near-identical key-prop items, nobody noticed that 17 keys the opposite of 13, 27 and 47. Nothing in the bank covers refs, portals, error boundaries, useLayoutEffect, transitions, custom hooks or Server Components.

Explanations argue against option numbers instead of against ideas. react-quiz-18, -48 and -49 name «option 1»/«Вариант 4» etc.; thirteen more say «The other options misunderstand...» without saying which claim is wrong or why. Both forms fail on the random-quiz route (positions are permuted), and the second form gives the reader nothing to learn from — the distractor's error is the most teachable part of a quiz item and it is systematically left unstated.
